body.text: Beijing has recently taken positive steps toward strengthening social insurance enforcement. A judicial interpretation by China’s Supreme People’s Court, which took effect in September 2025, made clear that agreements between employers and workers to waive social insurance contributions are invalid. On November 1, 2026, the State Taxation Administration began implementing nationwide standards for administrative penalties against social insurance violations. Under the new standards, employers that fail to pay social insurance contributions after being ordered to do so can face fines of up to three times the amount owed.

These penalties are not new, however; they were already established in China’s Social Insurance Law in 2011. Whether the new nationwide standards will lead to broader recovery of unpaid contributions remains to be seen.

Separately, Zhang Hui, director of the State Taxation Administration’s Beijing 12366 Taxpayer and Fee Payer Service Center, told China Business News in August that the effort to improve compliance with contribution bases focused mainly on large and medium-sized enterprises with the ability to pay. It addressed current contribution bases, without a campaign to collect historical arrears. Worker complaints concerning earlier years would be handled case by case.

Even so, the push for compliance has met resistance from both employers and workers. Some employers argue that with orders declining and profits shrinking, full contributions will force them to lay off workers or close their businesses. Some have already cut wages or shifted workers to outsourcing arrangements. Workers have doubts too. For those already earning low wages, contributions mean less take-home pay. Others question whether they will actually receive a pension after decades of contributions.
These doubts are not unfounded. They come from decades in which social insurance was treated as optional, and the results of that history are now visible.

The first generation of rural migrant workers who moved to cities to work in factories after China’s economic reforms are now in their 50s and 60s. China’s household registration system, known as hukou, has long tied access to social benefits to a person’s registered place of residence. Many migrant workers were never enrolled in the urban employee pension system.

One worker I know left home at 16 to work in factories in the cities. He worked there for 20 years. By his mid-30s, factories were no longer willing to hire him because of his age, so he returned to his hometown. He has since taken odd jobs there. Now 60, he was never enrolled in the employee pension system.

Many workers like him reach retirement age with only the basic pension for urban and rural residents, often around $30 a month, despite decades of work. When younger workers see this, it is not surprising that they doubt the system will work for them. The lack of adequate pensions for millions of older workers creates hardship for their families and poses risks to social stability.

Workers’ frustration is already visible. Employers’ failure to pay what they owe, whether wages or social insurance, has fueled growing unrest. According to Freedom House’s China Dissent Monitor, workers initiated approximately 2,500 recorded protests in China in 2025, many over unpaid wages. Workers accounted for 44 percent of all recorded protests in the third quarter of 2026.

The same insecurity also weighs on the economy. Workers with low incomes and unreliable pension and healthcare coverage have little choice but to save what they can. This is one reason China’s domestic consumption remains weak.

These problems share a common root: China’s long reliance on low-cost manufacturing. China’s rise as a manufacturing powerhouse has depended heavily on low wages. To attract investment, many local governments turned a blind eye when employers failed to pay social insurance contributions. According to a 2016 New York Times investigation, government documents showed that Zhengzhou authorities reduced Foxconn’s social insurance and other payments for workers by as much as $100 million a year to attract its investment.

Our own investigations show how widespread this remains. Of the more than 200 factories covered in our published reports, none made full social insurance contributions for their workers. In 2025, we investigated Foxconn’s Zhengzhou complex, Apple’s largest iPhone manufacturing site, which employed an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 workers during peak production. Workers we interviewed reported working 60 to 70 hours a week, and many said their employers had not made their full social insurance contributions.

This model has also helped fuel China’s enormous trade surplus. In the first three quarters of 2026, China’s merchandise trade surplus reached 6.46 trillion yuan, or more than $900 billion. Products made under these conditions are sold around the world, and international brands and consumers have shared the benefits of China’s low labor costs. But the surplus has become a growing source of international tension. The same model that keeps domestic consumption weak also deepens the trade imbalances that strain China’s relations with its partners.

Changing this model is a policy choice, not an impossibility. Before China’s Labor Contract Law took effect in 2008, some economists and business representatives warned that stronger labor protections would undermine the competitiveness of Chinese manufacturing. Yet China’s manufacturing sector and exports continued to expand in the years that followed. Tax authorities themselves now allow enterprises to reach compliance step by step over a reasonable period, showing that change can be gradual. And the Foxconn case shows that waiving social insurance was itself a decision made by local governments. With an enormous manufacturing sector and a massive trade surplus, China has no justification for treating unpaid social insurance as a means of staying export-competitive.

Raising wages and strengthening social insurance would increase costs for some businesses, but it would also give more households the confidence to spend. As Chinese households consume more at home, the economy could become less dependent on exports, and the trade surplus could begin to shrink.

For social insurance to support this economic rebalancing, enforcement must also reach smaller factories. Workers and society have already paid the price for decades of weak enforcement. Beijing can accept the costs of ensuring compliance now or face far greater social and economic costs later.
